questions.q: Why does « le garçon » need the cedilla?
choices: Without it, the c before o would be a k sound
It marks where the stress falls
It shows the n is silent
questions.why: c is hard before a, o, u and soft before e, i, y. The cedilla forces the soft s sound where the spelling would otherwise give k: ça, la leçon, le reçu.

questions.q: Is the u pronounced in « la guitare » ?
choices: No — it is only there to keep the g hard
No, and the g is soft anyway
questions.why: gu- and qu- are spelling devices: the u is silent. La guitare is "gee-tar", qui is "kee", not "kwee". Rare technical words like linguistique are the exceptions.

questions.q: Which of these has a z sound in the middle?
questions.why: A single s between two vowels is z; a double ss stays s. So le poison (poison) has z, le poisson (fish) has s. Same contrast as le désert and le dessert.

questions.q: How is the x pronounced in « l'exemple » ?
choices: gz, like the x of English "exam"
ks, like the x of English "text"
questions.why: ex- before a vowel is gz (exister, exact, l'examen); ex- before a consonant is ks (le texte, expliquer). At the end of a word, x is usually silent: le prix, la voix.

questions.q: Which letter is silent in « l'automne » ?
questions.why: The cluster mn simplifies to n, so l'automne ends like "tonn" and condamner loses its m too. French drops letters inside several fixed clusters.
-mpt- is said mt: compter, le comptable. Related fixed clusters: le doigt loses both g and t, and le cerf keeps only the r.

questions.q: Which of these words has an h aspiré, so it takes « le » and blocks liaison?
questions.why: h is never pronounced, but h aspiré behaves as if a consonant were there: no elision, no linking. There is no way to tell by looking — h aspiré words are mostly Germanic or English borrowings, and dictionaries mark them.

questions.q: Add the cedilla where it is needed: « le garcon ».
questions.why: Without the cedilla the c sits before o and would be read as k.

questions.q: « manger » keeps its soft g in the nous form by adding a letter. Complete: nous ___
questions.why: The e is inserted purely for pronunciation: g stays soft before e. Without it, mangons would have a hard g.

questions.q: Written « bage », the g would be soft. Add the one letter that makes it hard, giving the word for a ring: la ___
questions.why: gu- before e or i forces the hard g: la bague, le guide, longue. The u itself is never heard.

questions.q: Write « le » + « homme » as French actually writes it.
questions.why: The h of homme is mute, so the word behaves like a vowel and the article elides. Compare le hobby and le haut, where h aspiré blocks exactly this.
The single s sits between two vowels, so it is a z sound; the -on at the end is nasal. Written with s, heard as z.

questions.q: Say this out loud — two tricky consonants and two nasal vowels.
questions.why: ch is the English sh, and gn is the ni of "onion". Both nasals are full nasals: neither n is pronounced as a separate consonant.

questions.q: Say this out loud. Only two sounds survive out of five letters.
questions.why: -gt collapses: both the g and the t are silent, leaving "dwa". oi supplies the "wah".

questions.q: State the rule for when c and g are hard and when they are soft, and name the three spelling tricks French uses to override it.
a: c and g are hard before a, o, u and soft before e, i, y. Overrides: ç forces the soft c before a/o/u (le garçon); an inserted e keeps g soft before a/o (nous mangeons); gu- forces hard g before e/i (la guitare), and qu- spells the k sound before e/i (qui, quand).
questions.why: This one rule plus its three workarounds explains a large share of French spelling, including why verb stems change shape between forms.
